stem: The spouse caring for a client with advanced cancer says, 'I am sleeping only a few hours, missing work, and I am afraid I will make a mistake with the medications because I am exhausted.' Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.A: Assess the caregiver's current demands, available resources, and ability to perform care safely, then help identify support that matches the needs, such as sharing tasks, respite care, or social-work/counseling resources.
options.B: Encourage the spouse to continue all caregiving duties alone because accepting outside help generally increases caregiver burden.
options.C: Reassure the spouse that severe exhaustion is an expected part of caregiving and needs no intervention unless the client is hospitalized.
options.D: Focus only on the client's symptoms because caregiver sleep loss, work strain, and concerns about managing medications are unrelated to safe home care.

rationale: A is correct. NCI defines caregiver burden as stress or strain that occurs when caregiving demands exceed the resources available to the caregiver. Cancer caregivers can have emotional, social, financial, work-related, and health needs, and NCI emphasizes recognizing caregiver roles and challenges, asking what help is needed, sharing tasks, seeking support, and using respite or professional resources when appropriate. In this scenario, severe sleep loss plus concern about medication mistakes makes an assessment of caregiving capacity and available support clinically important. B is incorrect because NCI encourages caregivers to accept help and share responsibilities rather than assuming they must do everything alone. C inappropriately normalizes potentially unsafe exhaustion. D is incorrect because NCI treats caregiver well-being and ability to perform caregiving tasks as relevant to cancer care.
educational_objective: Recognize significant caregiver burden when caregiving demands exceed available resources and respond by assessing caregiver capacity and connecting the family with individualized practical, respite, and psychosocial support.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Informal Caregivers in Cancer (PDQ®) — Patient Version and Health Professional Version; Support for Caregivers of Cancer Patients; Taking Care of Yourself — Advanced Cancer and Caregivers
source_version_date: Current NCI PDQ and caregiver resources accessed 2026-08-18; Support for Caregivers of Cancer Patients updated 2025-02-03
source_locator: Informal Caregivers in Cancer Patient PDQ — 'Needs of Informal Caregivers' and 'Burdens of Being an Informal Caregiver' → definition of caregiver burden, emotional/social/financial needs, employment and role strain; Health Professional PDQ — 'Caregiver Burden', 'Secondary Appraisal: Resources for Informal Caregivers', and burden domains including disrupted schedule, financial problems, lack of support, and health problems; Support for Caregivers of Cancer Patients — 'Coping with Being a Cancer Caregiver', 'Ask for help from others', and counselor/social-worker support; Taking Care of Yourself — 'Use respite care'.
source_claim_supported: Caregiver burden occurs when caregiving demands exceed available resources; cancer caregivers may experience emotional, social, financial, employment, and health strain; clinicians should recognize caregiver needs and support task-sharing, respite, counseling/social-work, and other resources as appropriate.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Client Needs category 'Psychosocial Integrity' — nursing care that promotes and supports emotional, mental and social well-being; applied here to family/caregiver coping, support systems, stress management, therapeutic assessment and resource referral.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source definition-only caregiver-burden item into an applied home-care scenario where exhaustion threatens safe medication management. The final item assesses demands versus resources and individualizes support rather than mandating one service or merely naming caregiver burden.
audit_findings: Fresh NCI review directly defines caregiver burden as demands exceeding available resources and documents emotional, social, financial, employment and health effects.
The final key first assesses burden and safe caregiving capacity, then offers individualized—not mandatory—support options consistent with NCI caregiver guidance.
The medication-error concern is supplied by the caregiver in the stem, so the item does not infer a medication error has already occurred.
Distractors represent realistic unsafe responses: insisting on solo caregiving, normalizing severe exhaustion, and excluding caregiver capacity from home-care planning.
Independent adversarial review found no second answer, cueing, unsupported universal service requirement, source-locator defect, blueprint mismatch, or unresolved conflict.
